macro: This newsletter is a focused earnings note on Delta Air Lines rather than a broad market update. No index-level moves, risk tone, or overnight action are discussed. Macro context is limited to the demand environment for air travel, which remains resilient.
market_outlook: No explicit directional market view is provided by Adam in this note. The focus is entirely on Delta's Q3 results and what they signal for the airline sector.
bull_case: Delta's revenue grew 16% driven by RASM up 15%, reflecting strong pricing power with customers absorbing steep fare hikes without meaningful pushback. The Amex co-brand relationship remains healthy with remuneration up 15% year-over-year and double-digit growth in card acquisitions and spend. Q4 revenue guidance of plus 20% topped the Street's plus 18.4% estimate, signaling continued demand strength.

Non-fuel unit costs also rose 7.3% year-over-year, adding further cost pressure. Q4 EPS guidance midpoint of $1.40 is below consensus of $1.48, though Q4 revenue is expected to grow 20% versus the Street's 18.4% estimate. sectors: Airlines are under cost pressure from sharply higher fuel expenses, but demand and pricing power remain strong — a mixed picture for the sector heading into Q4.
tts_summary: Delta Air Lines reported third quarter results this morning and the headline read is mixed, leaning negative. On the top line, things looked strong — revenue grew 16% year over year, fueled by a 15% increase in revenue per available seat mile as the company pushed through steep fare hikes. Customers are absorbing those price increases without much pushback, which is a meaningful signal about the health of the consumer in the travel space. The Amex co-brand relationship also held up well, with remuneration climbing 15% year over year, and both card acquisitions and spend growing double digits. So demand is real and pricing power is intact. The problem is the cost side. Aggregate fuel expense exploded 62% to four point one billion dollars, and non-fuel unit costs rose 7.3% year over year. That combination overwhelmed the revenue strength and drove an earnings per share miss — Delta came in at one dollar and seventy-two cents versus the Street's estimate of one dollar and eighty-two cents. On guidance, the company gave a wide fourth quarter earnings per share range of one fifteen to one sixty-five. The midpoint of one forty is below the consensus of one forty-eight, which is going to sting. However, fourth quarter revenue is expected to surge 20%, ahead of the Street's eighteen point four percent estimate, so there is a silver lining on the top line. The bottom line here is that Delta's business fundamentally is in good shape — it is impressive that earnings were roughly flat year over year despite fuel costs up more than sixty percent. The company clearly has pricing power. But until fuel costs moderate, it is hard for that top-line strength to fully flow through to the bottom line. For traders, expect initial pressure on the stock given the earnings miss and the soft guidance midpoint, but watch whether bulls step in on the demand narrative and the revenue beat. This was purely an earnings note — no broad market color or Fed commentary was included in today's release.
